title: Irregular CPU load spikes with HAProxy 2.7.2
body:
### Detailed Description of the Problem

We are seeking the help of the community about a weird performance regression with our upgrade to HAProxy 2.7.2.

OS: ubuntu bionic (built using [this tool](https://github.com/cloudfoundry/bosh-linux-stemcell-builder))
SSL backend: openssl1

We deploy HAProxy as a load balancer in front of our platform. The backends are a stable set of routers that take care of sending the request to the right target application. We operate multiple deployments and on one of them in particular we noticed weird patterns in the CPU load. The pattern shows on other infrastructure providers as well, but it was most present on an Azure deployment. It started when we upgraded from 2.6.7 to 2.7.2. Other metrics (requests/s, sessions/s, front-/backend connections) didn't show any significant difference.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44866320/219028275-f3202dd9-84b9-4cc7-b376-8a08c08792c0.png)

As you can see in this graph, the load went from a stable percentage that fluctuates with the daily/weekly cycles of load on the platform to a wild mess. There are timeframes in which the VMs peak at 100% load. Taking a closer look at the graphs reveals an interesting pattern:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44866320/219028343-22b306dd-fe37-4a76-92e6-ad4b63f83ccc.png)

The HAProxies move around on certain "levels" of CPU load, each increase in load goes back down ~1h later. The jump up is roughly 25% which corresponds to one core on the VM. We run on 4 CPU 16 GB (or 8 GB, depending on the hyperscaler) VMs. Each VM has one HAProxy process running with `nbthread 4`. Since we have to update the `crt-list` from time to time we reload HAProxy using `SIGUSR2`. You can see the script that handles our HAProxy start/stop/reload in the [haproxy-boshrelease](https://github.com/cloudfoundry/haproxy-boshrelease/blob/master/jobs/haproxy/templates/haproxy_wrapper.erb) which is a wrapper that allows us to deploy HAProxy with [BOSH](https://bosh.io/docs/). Due to these reloads it can happen that multiple HAProxy processes are running at the same time. However, the older a reloaded process gets, the less load it sees. Overall it shouldn't get too much load in any case since most of load on our VMs is produced by TLS handshakes, which aren't done frequently on "old" processes.

It can also be observed that some HAProxy processes run at >300% CPU by themselves, without any additional HAProxy processes:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44866320/219028475-79aee539-8eab-4c6c-b6da-14457bf33c92.png)

Looking at such a process using the socket CLI shows that the HAProxy process itself is idle most of the time (`Idle_pct` >50%). Digging deeper and running `perf` showed this:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44866320/219028624-3db86ea0-0735-4f16-81b5-9cceb9b7899b.png)

I compared those values against an HAProxy running in a non-live isolated environment and couldn't reproduce the load pattern. However, the table that `perf` shows looks similar.

### Expected Behavior

CPU usage stays roughly the same (compared to before the upgrade) and there are no temporary spikes in HAProxy CPU usage.

### Steps to Reproduce the Behavior

Unknown

### Do you have any idea what may have caused this?

Most likely the upgrade to 2.7.2 since the other inputs that we observed didn't show significant changes.

### Do you have an idea how to solve the issue?

_No response_

Could be related to #1998

Questions:
- Are you aware of any changes that could've caused such issues?
- What do you recommend to troubleshoot such issues that cannot be reproduced on non-live environments?
- Is there any metric/socket-command we should take a closer look at?
- Any other third-party tool that can be used to better understand where those CPU cycles are consumed?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Looking at the perf output while running on a jammy (which brings openssl3 instead of openssl1) VM shows that the `BN_X931_generate_prime_ex` call is missing (which makes sense since it was removed in openssl3), however, we don't see a function that takes its place:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44866320/219049372-87d3ddb6-9473-4d22-8add-1f923aa40143.png)

CPU utilisation was still at around ~80% per core but this was done on an isolated dev deployment and also didn't show the CPU load pattern we saw in our live deployments.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: I suggest you stick with openssl 1.1.1, because multithreading performance in openssl 3.0 is terrible. Using openssl 3.0 here just muddies the waters and makes troubleshooting harder.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
It's not the first time I'm seeing "perf top" outputs showing only small numbers, I have no explanation for that. However in your case one crypto function seems expensive and makes me think that maybe you're experiencing much less connection reuse on the front side (or maybe the backend since you're using SSL there as well). It would be useful to send "show info;show activity" on the CLI twice 10s apart on both versions. It will show us the number of wakeups of various causes and the number of SSL handshakes on each side. Also please have a look in your stats page at the "sessions/total" column for your backend, when you hover the value, you'll get some details per status code and the reuse rate. It would be useful to compare between the two versions. Maybe for a reason I ignore we're not reusing certain connections.

Last point, since you appear to be running from the sources, please update to 2.7.3 as it fixes a vulnerability (as well as a few bugs).

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:

comments.author: participant3
comments.body: @participant2 Just recorded another spike around 75% CPU where we saw almost 10% of the recorded samples were spent in the `clock_gettime` function call. This was recorded using `perf top -g -p ` We are running HAproxy in master/worker mode and selected the worker pid for perf. Have you seen anything like this before? Does it look irregular? Fishing in the dark here.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Regarding clock_gettime I found a potential kernel bug for hyper-v. Since we are running on Azure here, I assume they are still using hyper-v as their hypervisor so it could be related: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=213029
However, the bug claims the regression in kernel 5.12, however we are running 
```
uname -r
5.15.0-58-generic
```

comments.author: participant3
comments.body: Here I have another perf run from a time (same config) when we don't see CPU spikes. We don't even see HAproxy at the top. Mostly kernel doing kernel stuff, sending packets etc. as you would expect. Noticable are the absence of `run_tasks_from_lists` and `clock_gettime` calls from the top 5 function calls.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
@participant3 your captures are extremely instructive! You're facing a bug by which a set of tasks wake up, do nothing and go back to sleep to instantly wake up again. The context-switch rate indicates 8.2 million such wakeups per second, and 58185 polling loops per second that are interrupted due to this activity. The long_rq indicator tells us that we're leaving process_runnable_tasks() with active tasks after having exhausted the maximum budget, but the run_queue indicates there's a single runnable task. So it makes me think that in fact there is exactly one task waking itself up so that it constantly has something to do and is wasting time there.

By issuing `show tasks` on this process you should see one function name taking roughly 100% of the CPU and it will tell us what this task is.

Given that perf top shows `sc_conn_io_cb()` taking a non-null amount of CPU, I strongly suspect it will be this one, and that it's involved in `h1_process_demux()` presence. However I have no idea why that would be the case at the moment!

Regarding your finding about `clock_gettime()` that's good to know. Here however it's just a byproduct of the loop being called a lot, hence the syscall is called a lot as well.

- front connections
- made over H1/SSL
- POST requests
- request still being uploaded
- response not sent yet
- h1c=0x400 (H1C_F_ERROR)
